meaning: “Without even doing …”: someone skips even the most basic step and goes straight to something else. Usually carries criticism, annoyance, or surprise.
connection: Verb masu-stem / suru-noun + もしないで (written: もせずに)

senses.label: Without even … (criticism)
senses.meaning: The most basic thing that should be done is skipped, and the next action happens anyway. The speaker usually sounds critical. 「も」 adds the sense of “not even this much”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + もしないで (見もしないで, 聞きもしないで); suru-noun + もしないで (確認もしないで)
examples: He started using the machine without even reading the manual.
Throwing it away without even looking inside — that's awful.
I ended up submitting the documents without even checking them.

senses.label: Not even stopping to … (devotion)
senses.meaning: Someone is so absorbed in something that they skip basics like sleeping or eating. This stresses their effort or dedication, so it is not always criticism.
senses.connection: 寝もしないで / 休みもしないで / 食べもしないで + verb
examples: My mother looked after me when I had a fever, without even sleeping.
He kept working all day without even taking a break.

senses.label: Written form: もせずに
senses.meaning: The written version of 「もしないで」 is 「もせずに」 or 「もせず」. Same meaning; common in news and novels.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem / suru-noun + もせず(に)
examples: He walked away without even looking back.
Drawing conclusions without proper research is dangerous.

notes: It attaches to the masu-stem (drop ます): 「見もしない」, 「聞きもしない」. With suru-verbs, say 「勉強もしない」, 「相談もしない」.
In 「何もしないで」 (without doing anything), 「も」 follows a question word. That is a different pattern.
「一時間もしないうちに」 (in less than an hour) is “quantity + もしない” and means a short time. It is not this pattern either.

daily.title: Complaining about family
daily.description: A mother complains that her child hands in homework without checking it.
daily.example: This kid hands in homework without even looking it over.

daily.title: Teasing a friend
daily.description: Your friend says it's impossible without trying, and you push back.
daily.example: Don't say it's impossible when you haven't even tried.

daily.title: Thanking for care
daily.description: Telling a friend how your family looked after you in hospital.
daily.example: While I was in hospital, my dad came every day without even taking a rest.

work.title: A boss scolds a subordinate
work.description: A subordinate sent an email without checking it.
work.example: Please stop sending emails without even checking the content.

work.title: Reading a news report
work.description: A report criticizes a company's hasty decision.
work.example: The company reportedly pushed ahead with the plan without sufficient review.

etymology: The masu-stem (used like a noun) + the emphatic particle 「も」 + 「しない」 + 「で」 (“in a state of not doing”). 「も」 singles out the action — “not even this” — giving “without even doing …”.

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: 「〜ないで」 neutrally says “do B without doing A”. 「〜もしないで」 adds 「も」 to stress that even the basic A was skipped, often with criticism.

similar.title: 〜もしない (not even)
similar.explanation: 「〜もしない」 ends the sentence: “doesn't even do …”. 「〜もしないで」 continues to another action: “without even doing …, (did B)”.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: 「〜ずに」 is the written form of 「ないで」. Likewise 「もせずに」 is the written form of 「もしないで」, with the same “not even” emphasis.

meaning: Attaches to a noun to mean “on par with …, at the level of …”, as in 「プロ並み」 or 「平年並み」.
connection: Noun + 並み (の + noun / に / だ)

senses.label: On par with …
senses.meaning: The degree or level is about the same as some standard: “as good as …”, “like a …”. Often used as praise for a level higher than expected.
senses.connection: Noun + 並みの + noun / 並みに + verb or adjective / 並みだ (プロ並み, 大人並み, 一流並み)
examples: His cooking is as good as a professional's.
This child eats as much as an adult.
This hotel offers service on par with a luxury hotel.

senses.label: About the same as usual
senses.meaning: 「平年並み」, 「例年並み」 and 「前年並み」 are set phrases in weather forecasts and statistics. They mean “about the same as an average year / last year”.
senses.connection: 平年 / 例年 / 前年 + 並み
examples: This summer's temperatures are expected to be around normal.
Sales stayed at about the same level as last year.

senses.label: Like ordinary people
senses.meaning: 「人並み」 and 「世間並み」 mean “like most people, ordinary”. Often used modestly about one's own life or ability.
senses.connection: 人並み / 世間並み + の + noun / に
examples: If I can live a normal life, that's enough for me.
I'd like to get married and have a family, like most people.

notes: 「並み」 attaches only to nouns, not to verbs or adjectives.
In 「町並み」 (streetscape), 「家並み」 and 「足並み」, 「並み」 means “a row”. 「月並み」 means “commonplace”. These are not this pattern.
It can also be written in kana: 「プロなみ」.

daily.title: Praising a friend's baking
daily.description: A friend serves you a cake they made.
daily.example: This cake is as good as one from a shop.

daily.title: Watching the forecast
daily.description: The weather forecast gives tomorrow's temperature.
daily.example: Tomorrow's high will be around normal for this time of year.

daily.title: Talking about life goals
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about the future.
daily.example: I don't need luxury — just to live like everyone else.

work.title: Evaluating a new hire
work.description: A manager praises a new employee.
work.example: His English is on par with a native speaker's.

work.title: Reading business news
work.description: A report on a company's results.
work.example: Profits this term held at about the same level as last year.

etymology: From the verbs 「並ぶ」 / 「並む」 (to line up). “Standing in the same row” came to mean “on the same level”, and it became a suffix meaning “equal to …”.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (degree)
similar.explanation: 「くらい」 attaches to many word types and shows degree by comparison. 「並み」 attaches only to nouns and means “reaching the level of a standard”.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 「〜のようだ」 is a simile, “like …”, not necessarily about level. 「〜並み」 focuses on being at the same level.

similar.title: 〜と同じ
similar.explanation: 「と同じ」 means exactly the same. 「並み」 means roughly the same level, often as praise: “as good as …”.

title: 〜なんという／なんと〜 (exclamation)
meaning: Expresses strong admiration or surprise: “What a …!”, “How …!”, “Believe it or not, …”.
connection: なんという + noun (だ); なんと + adjective / verb + ことか / のだろう

senses.label: What a …!
senses.meaning: 「なんという + noun」 shows strong feeling about something in front of you, good or bad. 「なんということだ」 often means shock or dismay: “How could this happen?”
senses.connection: なんという + noun + だ / でしょう (なんという美しさだ, なんということだ)
examples: What a beautiful view!
Oh no, how could this happen? It's all gone.

senses.label: How …!
senses.meaning: 「なんと〜ことか / のだろう」 pours out emotion. It is written and a bit literary. In speech, 「なんて」 is more common.
senses.connection: なんと + i-adjective / na-adjective / verb + ことか / のだろう / ことだろう
examples: What a wonderful performance!
How precious peaceful everyday life is!

senses.label: Believe it or not
senses.meaning: 「なんと」 at the start of a sentence or before a number shows surprise at something unexpected. Common when reporting a surprising fact.
senses.connection: なんと、+ sentence; なんと + number
examples: Believe it or not, those two are apparently getting married.
A whopping 100,000 people came to this event.

notes: 「なんという名前ですか」 is a real question (“What is it called?”), not an exclamation.
「なんとか」 (somehow), 「なんとなく」 (for some reason) and 「なんと言っても」 (after all) are different expressions.
In conversation, 「なんて」 is more common: 「なんてきれいなんだろう」.

daily.title: Sightseeing
daily.description: Watching the sunrise from a mountaintop.
daily.example: How beautiful!

daily.title: Sharing big news
daily.description: Telling your family something unexpected.
daily.example: Guess what — I won the lottery!

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character's monologue after a disaster.
daily.example: How could this happen? There's no undoing it now.

work.title: Product promotion
work.description: Ad copy highlights an amazing number.
work.example: In just one month after launch, we sold an incredible one million units.

work.title: Giving a speech
work.description: Expressing thanks at an awards ceremony.
work.example: How reassuring your support has been to me!

etymology: 「なんと」 comes from the question word 「何（なに）」, shortened to 「なん」, plus the particle 「と」; originally “how, in what way”. From the rhetorical “How could this be?” it came to express wonder and surprise. 「なんという」 is literally 「何という」 — “what can one say”.

similar.title: 〜なんて
similar.explanation: 「なんて」 is the casual form. It can start an exclamation or follow a clause to mean “to think that …!”. 「なんと / なんという」 sound more written and formal.

similar.title: 〜ことか
similar.explanation: 「〜ことか」 itself means “how …!”, and is often paired with 「なんと」 or 「どんなに」.

similar.title: 〜とは (surprise)
similar.explanation: 「〜とは」 comes at the end and expresses shock at a fact. 「なんと」 comes first and leads into the surprising content.

title: 〜に (addition / combination)
meaning: 「AにB」 means “A with B” or “A plus B”: a standard combination or an added item.

senses.label: Classic combination
senses.meaning: Two things that commonly go together, like “A with B”. Many proverbs use this form.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun (ご飯にみそ汁, 梅に鶯, 鬼に金棒)
examples: The classic Japanese breakfast is rice with miso soup.
That team with that coach — it's like giving a demon an iron club. They're unstoppable.

senses.label: Plus, and
senses.meaning: When ordering or listing, it means “A, plus B”. Casual and common in speech.
senses.connection: Noun + に + noun + を / が (コーヒーにケーキを)
examples: A coffee and a slice of cake, please.
For dinner I made curry and a salad.

notes: For three or more items, use 「AにBにC」. See “〜に〜に (listing)”.
This 「に」 only links nouns. There is no verb taking a target or destination, so don't confuse it with the 「に」 of destination or indirect object.

daily.title: Ordering at a café
daily.description: A customer orders a drink and a dessert.
daily.example: Black tea and cheesecake, please.

daily.title: Talking about outfits
daily.description: A friend comments on your clothes.
daily.example: A white shirt with jeans — simple and nice.

work.title: Preparing meeting snacks
work.description: Coworkers decide what to serve at a meeting.
work.example: For the meeting, tea and rice crackers should be fine, right?

etymology: The case particle 「に」 originally marks where something attaches or arrives. From “attached onto something” came the meaning “A with B added on”.

similar.title: 〜に加えて
similar.explanation: 「に加えて」 is a written “in addition to”, followed by a full clause. 「AにB」 simply pairs two nouns.

similar.title: 〜に〜に (listing)
similar.explanation: 「AにBに」 lists several items: “A, and B, and …”. This entry is mostly about a pair that goes together.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「や」 gives a partial list: “A, B, and so on”. 「に」 presents the two as a set.

meaning: “Even after things have gone as far as …, still …”. Usually critical or disapproving.
connection: Noun / verb dictionary form + に至っても

senses.label: Even when it comes to …
senses.meaning: The first part is a serious situation that should prompt action. The second part says nothing changed or no action was taken. Formal and written, often critical or regretful.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に至っても; noun + に至っても (+ なお / まだ)
examples: Even after people died, the company took no safety measures.
Even now that things have come to this, the government won't act.
Even when it went to court, he never apologized.

senses.label: Even now
senses.meaning: 「今に至っても」 and 「今日に至っても」 mean “even now, still …”. It stresses that a state has not changed for a long time.
senses.connection: 今 / 現在 / 今日 + に至っても (+ なお)
examples: The cause of the accident is still unknown even today.
Even now, I can't forget that day.

notes: The second part is usually negative or “unchanged”, often with 「なお」, 「まだ」 or 「依然として」.
Written style, common in news and opinion pieces. In speech, use 「〜になっても」.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: A report criticizes a company's response.
daily.example: Even as the damage spread, there was no explanation at all.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: A friend keeps ignoring warnings.
daily.example: Even now that his doctor has told him to stop, he won't quit smoking.

work.title: Opinion article
work.description: A commentator criticizes slow management.
work.example: Even after three straight years of losses, management didn't change course.

work.title: Report
work.description: An investigation notes the problem remains.
work.example: Even now, no fundamental solution has been reached.

etymology: 「至る」 means “to reach”. 「に至って」 is “having reached a certain point”; add the concessive 「ても」 and you get “even having reached this point, …”.

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: 「に至って（はじめて）」 means “only when it came to …, finally …” (a natural result). 「に至っても」 is the opposite: “even at this point, still not …”.

similar.title: 〜に至っては
similar.explanation: 「に至っては」 introduces the most extreme example: “as for …, it's even worse”. 「に至っても」 stresses that nothing changed despite the serious situation.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: 「にもかかわらず」 is a general “despite …”. 「に至っても」 stresses that things have reached an extreme.

meaning: “Associated with …, surrounding …”. Mostly used with legends, stories, and anecdotes.

senses.label: Stories and legends about …
senses.meaning: The most typical use: stories, legends, or secrets that surround a person, place, or object. It has a slightly mysterious, intriguing feel.
senses.connection: Noun + にまつわる + 伝説 / 話 / エピソード / 謎
examples: I heard a strange legend about this temple.
My grandmother told me memories connected to this old clock.

senses.label: Related to …
senses.meaning: Today it is also used broadly for “about …”, often in book titles, TV shows and article headings. It sounds more story-like than 「に関する」.
senses.connection: Noun + にまつわる + トラブル / 問題 / 話題 / 雑学
examples: Trouble involving money happens all around us.
Today, let's talk about topics related to Japanese food.
Here's a story about how the name came about.

notes: It is almost always used as 「Aにまつわる + noun」 to modify a noun. 「にまつわって」 is rare.
The kanji is 「纏わる」, but it is usually written in kana.
The verb 「まつわりつく」 means “to cling to”, as in 「子どもが母親にまつわりつく」. That is not this pattern.

daily.title: Sightseeing
daily.description: A guide introduces an old castle to tourists.
daily.example: There's a sad story connected to this castle.

daily.title: Watching TV
daily.description: A friend recommends a trivia show.
daily.example: That show on animal trivia was really interesting.

daily.title: Reading a book
daily.description: A book's title and blurb.
daily.example: This book unravels the mysteries surrounding famous paintings.

work.title: Pitching a feature
work.description: An editor proposes a special feature at a meeting.
work.example: For the next issue, I'd like to run a feature on local festivals.

work.title: Legal consultation
work.description: A law firm's website describes its services.
work.example: We offer consultations on matters related to inheritance.

etymology: 「まつわる」 (纏わる) originally means “to wind around, to cling”. From “winding around something” it came to mean “connected to, surrounding something”.

similar.title: 〜に関して・〜に関する
similar.explanation: 「に関する」 is a neutral, objective “about”. 「にまつわる」 has a story-like feel and goes with legends, anecdotes and memories.

similar.title: 〜にかかわる
similar.explanation: 「にかかわる」 usually means “affecting (something serious like life or honor)”. 「にまつわる」 means “(stories, topics) surrounding …”.

similar.title: 〜をめぐって
similar.explanation: 「をめぐって」 is usually about disputes or conflicts over something. 「にまつわる」 just refers to related stories or topics.

meaning: “Can't bear to …”: out of pity or attachment, one can't bring oneself to do something.
connection: Verb dictionary form + に忍びない

senses.label: Can't bring oneself to
senses.meaning: Out of sympathy, pity or attachment, one can't bear to do something. Often with 「捨てる」, 「断る」 or 「切る」. Formal and written.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + に忍びない (捨てるに忍びない, 断るに忍びない)
examples: These clothes are full of memories, so I can't bear to throw them away.
When she begged me like that, I couldn't bring myself to say no.

senses.label: Too painful to watch / hear
senses.meaning: 「見るに忍びない」 and 「聞くに忍びない」 are set phrases. The scene is so tragic or pitiful that you can't bear to look or listen.
senses.connection: 見る / 聞く + に忍びない
examples: The state of the disaster area was too painful to look at.
The bereaved families' stories were almost too painful to listen to.

notes: It usually follows a small set of verbs like 「見る」, 「聞く」, 「捨てる」 and 「断る」. It's an emotional, written expression.
「見るに堪えない」 means “so bad you can't watch it” (disgust). 「見るに忍びない」 means “so pitiful you can't bear to watch” (sympathy).
Forms like 「忍びなく」 and 「忍びず」 are also used: 「捨てるに忍びなく、取っておいた」.

daily.title: Decluttering
daily.description: You can't throw away your child's old toys.
daily.example: I can't bear to throw away the toys from when my kids were little.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: Talking with family about an injured animal on the news.
daily.example: That puppy was so pitiful I could hardly watch.

work.title: Personnel decision
work.description: A manager talks about layoffs.
work.example: It pains me to let go of employees who served us for years, but there's no other choice.

work.title: Formal letter
work.description: Politely declining a request in a formal letter.
work.example: It truly pains us not to meet your expectations, but we must decline this time.

etymology: 「忍ぶ」 means “to endure, to bear”. 「〜に忍びない」 is literally “cannot endure doing …”, so “can't bear to”. 「忍びない」 alone can also mean “to feel bad about”.

similar.title: 〜に堪える
similar.explanation: 「見るに堪えない」 means the content is so bad you can't watch (disgust). 「見るに忍びない」 means it's so pitiful you can't bear to watch (sympathy).

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: 「かねる」 means “unable to … (because of one's position)”, often a polite refusal. 「に忍びない」 is about being emotionally unable to do it.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: 「てたまらない」 means a feeling is unbearably strong. 「に忍びない」 means you can't bring yourself to do an action out of pity.

meaning: Says that an explanation, plan or approach is “a stretch, unreasonable, doesn't hold up”.
connection: Noun + には無理がある; verb dictionary form / plain form + の(に)は無理がある

senses.label: Far-fetched, doesn't add up
senses.meaning: An explanation, interpretation or premise is not logical. Used to disagree or criticize politely.
senses.connection: Noun + には無理がある (説明, 設定, 解釈, 理屈); 〜と考えるのには無理がある
examples: I think that explanation is a bit of a stretch.
It's hard to believe he did it all by himself.
The premise of this drama is far-fetched.

senses.label: Unrealistic, hard to pull off
senses.meaning: A plan or schedule is hard to achieve under the conditions. Softer than saying 「無理だ」 outright.
senses.connection: Noun + に(は)無理がある (計画, 日程, 予算); verb dictionary form + には無理がある
examples: Planning to finish it in one week is unrealistic.
Covering everything with this budget is a stretch.

notes: It often comes with 「少し」, 「やや」, 「かなり」 or 「どうしても」 to adjust how strong the criticism is.
Softer than 「無理だ」, so it suits meetings and reviews where you point out a problem politely.
「〜のも無理はない」 means something completely different: “no wonder, it's natural that …”.

daily.title: Discussing a movie with friends
daily.description: Complaining about the plot after a film.
daily.example: The twist that the culprit was a twin is way too far-fetched.

daily.title: Family plans
daily.description: The family discusses weekend plans.
daily.example: Isn't visiting three places in one day a bit much?

work.title: Raising a concern in a meeting
work.description: Politely voicing concern about a boss's schedule.
work.example: I'm afraid this schedule may be somewhat unrealistic.

work.title: Peer review
work.description: A reviewer points out a problem in a paper's reasoning.
work.example: Drawing this conclusion from these data is a stretch.

etymology: 「無理」 literally means “without reason (理)”, i.e. “unreasonable”, and extends to “impossible, forced”. 「〜には無理がある」 is literally “there is something unreasonable in …”.

similar.title: 〜のも無理はない
similar.explanation: 「のも無理はない」 means “no wonder”, accepting the other side. 「には無理がある」 means “unreasonable, a stretch”, rejecting it.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: 「わけがない」 is a strong “there's no way”. 「には無理がある」 just politely notes that something doesn't quite hold up.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: 「かねる」 says the speaker finds it hard to do something. 「には無理がある」 judges the claim or plan itself as unreasonable.

meaning: The same noun is repeated to mean “… after …, over and over”, stressing accumulation.
connection: Noun A + に + noun A + を重ねて / を重ねる

senses.label: Repeated effort
senses.meaning: Effort, study or improvement is made again and again. Used to show a result was hard-won. Often followed by 「〜た結果」, 「〜た末に」 or 「完成した」.
senses.connection: 改良 / 検討 / 工夫 / 苦労 / 練習 + に + the same noun + を重ねて
examples: After improvement upon improvement, the new product was finally finished.
After careful deliberation, we decided to cancel the plan.
Through hardship after hardship, he grew his shop.

senses.label: Going from bad to worse
senses.meaning: With negative things, bad things pile up and get worse — like telling more lies to cover a lie.
senses.connection: 嘘 / 失敗 / 借金 / 無理 + に + the same noun + を重ねる
examples: He piled lie upon lie and finally lost everyone's trust.
I want to escape a life of borrowing to pay off borrowing.

notes: The two nouns are usually identical; the repetition stresses “again and again”.
Mostly written or fairly formal; common when describing experiences and achievements.
「年を重ねる」 and 「経験を重ねる」 just mean “to accumulate”. They lack the 「AにA」 repetition, so they aren't this pattern.

daily.title: Talking about a parent's efforts
daily.description: Telling a friend how your father opened his shop.
daily.example: My dad went through hardship after hardship to open this shop.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character keeps lying and gets trapped.
daily.example: As he piled lie upon lie, he reached the point of no return.

work.title: Product launch
work.description: The lead developer describes the development process.
work.example: This is a product we're proud of — the result of our team's trial and error and countless improvements.

work.title: Company announcement
work.description: A company announces a difficult decision.
work.example: After extensive discussions, we have decided to withdraw from this business.

etymology: 「重ねる」 means “to stack, to repeat”. 「AにAを重ねる」 is literally “stack another A on top of A”, a vivid way to show repeated build-up.

similar.title: 〜に〜て／〜に〜た (repetition)
similar.explanation: 「待ちに待った」 and 「考えに考えた」 repeat a verb stem to stress intensity. 「〜に〜を重ねて」 repeats a noun to stress the number of times.

similar.title: 〜末(に)
similar.explanation: 「末に」 means “after …, finally”. It often follows this pattern: 「検討に検討を重ねた末に」.

similar.title: 〜を経て
similar.explanation: 「を経て」 simply means going through a stage or process. 「〜に〜を重ねて」 stresses repetition many times.

meaning: “I wonder …”: a puzzled, worried or resigned remark, often said to oneself.
connection: (question word …) verb / adjective plain form + のやら / ものやら / ことやら

senses.label: I wonder … (のやら)
senses.meaning: Expresses puzzlement about something unclear. Often paired with 「何」, 「いつ」, 「どこ」 or 「いったい」. Often a hint of annoyance or helplessness.
senses.connection: Question word … plain form + のやら (na-adjective / noun: なのやら)
examples: What on earth is that kid thinking?
Who knows where he went — I can't reach him.

senses.label: What should I do? (ものやら)
senses.meaning: 「〜たものやら」 and 「〜ばいいものやら」 mean not knowing what to do; being at a loss.
senses.connection: どう + verb ta-form + ものやら; どう + verb ば-form + いいものやら
examples: How on earth should I explain this situation?
I have no idea where to even begin.

senses.label: What will become of it? (ことやら)
senses.meaning: 「どうなることやら」 and 「いつになることやら」 are set phrases. They express worry or pessimism about the future.
senses.connection: どうなる / いつになる + ことやら; いつのことやら
examples: I'm so worried about what will happen from here.
Who knows when the house will ever be finished.

notes: Mostly used when talking to oneself or at the end of a sentence; 「分からない」 is often left out after it.
「〜やら〜やら」 lists things (“what with … and …”), with no question. 「〜のやら〜のやら」 means “not sure whether … or …”. Keep them apart.
It sounds a little old-fashioned and written. In conversation, 「〜んだろう」 or 「〜かな」 are more common.

daily.title: Worried about a child
daily.description: A mother worries because her child is home late.
daily.example: Where is he and what is he doing at this hour?

daily.title: Facing a tough problem
daily.description: Talking to yourself over difficult homework.
daily.example: A problem this hard — how am I supposed to solve it?

daily.title: Complaining in a chat
daily.description: Talking with a friend about never-ending construction.
daily.example: Who knows when the construction in front of the station will ever end.

work.title: Stalled project
work.description: Coworkers discuss a project's prospects.
work.example: Now the budget's been cut too — who knows what'll become of this project.

work.title: Reading an opinion piece
work.description: An article doubts a policy.
work.example: Whether this policy will actually work remains in doubt.

etymology: 「やら」 is a contraction of 「にやあらむ」 (“might it be …?”), via 「やらん」. So it carries a built-in tone of uncertainty.

similar.title: 〜のやら〜のやら
similar.explanation: 「AのやらBのやら」 gives two possibilities: “not sure if it's A or B”. This entry expresses puzzlement about one thing.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: 「のだろうか」 is a neutral question to oneself. 「のやら」 adds stronger helplessness, confusion or annoyance.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「AやらBやら」 lists things: “what with A and B”. It is not a question.

meaning: Lists two opposite or different possibilities: “whether … or …, who knows”. Shows confusion or annoyance.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form + のやら + plain form + のやら (na-adjective / noun: なのやら)

senses.label: Yes or no?
senses.meaning: Pairs the positive and negative of the same action: “can't tell whether they will or not”. Often shows annoyance at someone being vague. Often followed by 「わからない」 or 「はっきりしない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のやら + verb nai-form + のやら
examples: He won't say clearly whether he's coming or not.
I have no idea whether my son is studying or not.

senses.label: A or B?
senses.meaning: Lists two different states or possibilities that are hard to tell apart. Often used for someone who is hard to read.
senses.connection: Plain form A + のやら + plain form B + のやら
examples: I can't tell from her face whether she's happy or angry.
I never know if he's serious or joking.

notes: The second part is often 「わからない」, 「はっきりしない」 or 「見当がつかない」, and is sometimes left out.
Unlike the listing pattern 「〜やら〜やら」 (“what with … and …”), this one has 「の」 and expresses doubt.

daily.title: Waiting for a friend's reply
daily.description: A friend still hasn't said if they're coming to the party.
daily.example: That guy won't even reply — no idea if he's coming or not.

daily.title: A child's reaction
daily.description: Parents can't tell if their child likes the present.
daily.example: Hard to tell whether he likes the present or not — he barely reacted.

work.title: Vague client
work.description: Reporting a client's reaction to the boss.
work.example: It's unclear whether they intend to sign the contract or not.

work.title: Reading a news commentary
work.description: A commentator criticizes the government's vague stance.
work.example: The government is avoiding a clear answer on whether it will raise taxes or not.

etymology: The doubtful 「やら」 (from 「にやあらむ」) follows the nominalizer 「の」 to make 「のやら」. Placing two of them side by side shows being unable to decide between two possibilities.

similar.title: 〜のやら・〜ものやら・〜ことやら
similar.explanation: A single 「のやら」 expresses doubt about one thing. 「AのやらBのやら」 gives two possibilities and says you can't tell which.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: 「AやらBやら」 lists things, like 「泣くやら笑うやら」 (crying and laughing). This pattern has 「の」 and means “not sure if A or B”.

similar.title: 〜かどうか
similar.explanation: 「かどうか」 is a neutral “whether or not”. 「のやら〜のやら」 adds the speaker's confusion or annoyance.

meaning: Something important is coming up soon: “with … just ahead”. It can also mean physically having something close behind.
connection: Noun + を (time word + に) 控えて / 控えた + noun

senses.label: With … coming up
senses.meaning: An important event — an exam, a match, a wedding — is just around the corner. Often 「AをBに控えて」, where B is a time word like “tomorrow” or “next month”. The second part is usually preparation or current feelings.
senses.connection: Noun + を + time word + に控えて; noun + を控えた + noun
examples: With the entrance exam tomorrow, my son is nervous.
My sister, whose wedding is next month, seems busy every day.
With the final coming up, the players began their last preparations.

senses.label: Written: 〜を控え、
senses.meaning: News reports often use the continuative 「〜を控え、」. It describes what is happening on the eve of a major event.
senses.connection: Noun + を控え、+ clause
examples: With the general election approaching, the parties are becoming more active.
With the shareholders' meeting coming up, management is scrambling to prepare.

senses.label: Backed by, close to
senses.meaning: Something like a mountain or the sea is right behind or next to a place. Mostly in written descriptions of scenery.
senses.connection: (背後に) 山 / 海 + を控えた + noun
examples: It's a quiet hot-spring town with mountains at its back.

notes: 「控える」 also means “to refrain from”, as in 「お酒を控える」 or 「外出を控える」. That is not this pattern; tell them apart by the noun before it.
The noun before it is usually a big upcoming event: an exam, a match, an election, a wedding.

daily.title: Nervous before an exam
daily.description: A student explains how they've been lately.
daily.example: With the entrance exam a week away, I can't even sleep at night.

daily.title: Family news
daily.description: Telling a relative that your sister is about to give birth.
daily.example: My sister is due soon, so she's come back to stay with our parents.

work.title: Reading the news
work.description: A report on the eve of a sports event.
work.example: With the opening just days away, preparations at the venue are moving at full speed.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Explaining to a client why the company is busy.
work.example: We are currently preparing for a new product launch, so our responses are delayed.

etymology: 「控える」 originally means “to wait nearby, to stand by”. From “something is waiting right beside you” came “something is about to happen” and, spatially, “close by”. Separately it developed the meaning “to hold back, to refrain”.

similar.title: 〜に先立って
similar.explanation: 「に先立って」 means “prior to … (do something first)”, focusing on the action beforehand. 「を控えて」 focuses on the event being imminent.

similar.title: 〜矢先に
similar.explanation: 「矢先に」 means something unexpected happened just as you were about to do something. 「を控えて」 just means an event is near.

similar.title: 〜に向けて
similar.explanation: 「に向けて」 means preparing with something as a goal. 「を控えて」 means the event is already right in front of you.

meaning: “Taking … as an opportunity”: something becomes the trigger to start a new action or make a change.
connection: Noun + を機に / を機として; verb ta-form + の + を機に

senses.label: Taking … as a chance
senses.meaning: A turning point in life or society becomes the chance to start something new or make a change. Usually a positive, deliberate decision. More formal than 「をきっかけに」.
senses.connection: Noun + を機に (結婚, 就職, 退職, 転勤, 入学); 〜たの + を機に
examples: When I got married, I quit my job and moved back to my hometown.
Getting sick was my chance to quit smoking.
When I joined the company, I started living on my own.

senses.label: Taking this opportunity
senses.meaning: 「これを機に」 is a common set phrase. Used in speeches and letters: “taking this opportunity, (from now on) …”.
senses.connection: これ + を機に + 今後とも / ぜひ etc.
examples: Taking this opportunity, we look forward to working with you in the future.
Why not take this opportunity to rethink your health?

notes: The second part is usually the speaker's own deliberate action or decision, or a clear change.
More formal than 「をきっかけに」 and a bit less stiff than 「を契機に」. Common in business emails and speeches.
「機」 is read 「き」, not 「はた」.

daily.title: Explaining a move
daily.description: Telling a friend why you moved.
daily.example: When our kid started elementary school, we moved to the suburbs.

daily.title: New Year's resolution
daily.description: Chatting with family about your plans for the year.
daily.example: With the new year, I've decided to go jogging every morning.

work.title: Farewell speech
work.description: A speech at a farewell party for a transfer.
work.example: With this transfer, I want to take on new fields as well.

work.title: Business email
work.description: A greeting after a first collaboration.
work.example: Taking this opportunity, we sincerely hope for a long relationship.

etymology: 「機」 means “opportunity, the right moment”, as in 「機会」 and 「契機」. 「を機に」 is literally “taking … as the moment”.

similar.title: 〜をきっかけに
similar.explanation: 「きっかけ」 is more casual and works for small chance events. 「を機に」 is more formal and used for major turning points in life.

similar.title: 〜を契機に
similar.explanation: 「を契機に」 is the most formal, often for big social or historical changes. 「を機に」 is common for personal decisions and business settings.

similar.title: 〜を境に
similar.explanation: 「を境に」 stresses a sharp before/after change, usually one that just happens. 「を機に」 is usually about starting something new on purpose.

meaning: “With … as the dividing line”: things change clearly before and after a point. It can also mark a physical boundary.
connection: Noun + を境に(して) / を境として

senses.label: Turning point
senses.meaning: Before and after a certain time or event, things are completely different. The second part is usually “changed completely” or “started to …”. The change often just happens, not necessarily by choice.
senses.connection: Time / event noun + を境に(して) (あの日, 事故, その日, 震災)
examples: Ever since that accident, he became a completely different person.
Once I turned 40, my stamina suddenly dropped.
From that day on, the two stopped speaking to each other.

senses.label: Boundary line
senses.meaning: A river, mountain range or road serves as a physical boundary. The second part is usually “is divided into …” or “is different”.
senses.connection: Place noun + を境に (川, 山, 県境, 道路)
examples: With this river as the border, the east is Osaka and the west is Hyogo.
The weather is completely different on either side of the mountains.

notes: The second part is usually a change or a difference, with a clear contrast between before and after.
「境」 is read 「さかい」. You can also say 「〜を境目に」.
It stresses the dividing point, not intention. For deliberate decisions, 「を機に」 is more common.

daily.title: Looking back
daily.description: Telling a friend how you changed.
daily.example: Studying abroad really changed the way I think.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Small talk with a neighbor as the seasons change.
daily.example: It suddenly got cold starting yesterday, didn't it?

work.title: Analyzing data
work.description: An analyst explains sales figures at a meeting.
work.example: Since April, sales have been rising sharply.

work.title: Reading a history book
work.description: A history book describes major social change.
work.example: This war marked a turning point that transformed people's lives.

etymology: 「境」 means “border, boundary”, as in 「国境」 and 「県境」. 「を境に」 is literally “taking … as the border”, extended from physical boundaries to points in time.

similar.title: 〜を機に
similar.explanation: 「を機に」 usually means seizing a chance to start something on purpose. 「を境に」 stresses a sharp before/after contrast, usually a change that just happens.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: 「てからというもの」 means “ever since …, (it's been) …”, following a te-form. 「を境に」 follows a noun and stresses the dividing point.

similar.title: 〜を皮切りに
similar.explanation: 「を皮切りに」 means “starting with …, similar things followed one after another”. 「を境に」 means things changed before and after that point.

meaning: “On the premise of …”: taking a condition as given and acting or judging on that basis.
connection: Noun + を前提として / を前提に; plain form + こと + を前提として

senses.label: On the premise of
senses.meaning: Doing something, dating someone, or making a plan with a certain condition as the basis. Formal and written. 「を前提に」 is also common.
senses.connection: Noun + を前提として / を前提に + verb
examples: Please go out with me with marriage in mind.
This system operates on the condition that the person consents.

senses.label: … premised on …
senses.meaning: 「〜を前提とした + noun」 and 「〜を前提とする + noun」 modify a noun: “… based on the premise of …”.
senses.connection: Noun + を前提とした / を前提とする + noun
examples: This curriculum is designed for students planning to study abroad.
This training assumes you will be hired as a full-time employee.

senses.label: Assuming that …
senses.meaning: With 「〜ことを前提に」, you first assume a situation is true and then plan or judge. Common in business and academic settings.
senses.connection: Plain form + こと + を前提として / を前提に
examples: We made the plan assuming everyone would take part.
We need to draw up the budget on the assumption that prices will rise.

notes: 「を前提に」 and 「を前提として」 mean the same; the former is shorter, the latter more formal.
「〜という前提で」 is also common: 「明日晴れるという前提で準備する」.
Mostly used in business, legal and academic settings.

daily.title: Dating seriously
daily.description: A man tells his girlfriend's parents he is serious.
daily.example: I'm seeing your daughter with marriage in mind.

daily.title: Apartment hunting
daily.description: A real-estate agent explains the conditions to a tenant.
daily.example: This apartment is offered on the condition that you stay two years or more.

work.title: Project meeting
work.description: The project lead explains the plan's assumptions.
work.example: This plan assumes that the budget will be approved.

work.title: Recruitment info
work.description: HR explains the nature of an internship.
work.example: This internship does not guarantee a job offer.

etymology: 「前提」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “prerequisite”, originally a logic term (the starting point of an argument). 「〜を前提とする」 means “to take … as the premise”; 「として」 is the te-form of 「とする」.

similar.title: 〜を前提に／〜を前提として
similar.explanation: Both mean the same. 「を前提に」 is the shorter form; 「を前提として」 is more formal.

similar.title: 〜上で
similar.explanation: 「〜た上で」 means “after doing …, then …”, stressing order. 「を前提として」 stresses a condition or assumption.

similar.title: 〜を踏まえて
similar.explanation: 「を踏まえて」 means acting based on existing facts or results. 「を前提として」 is often based on conditions or assumptions not yet confirmed.
